title: Shining the light on cotyledon and true leaf adaxial and abaxial stomatal patterns. A commentary on ‘Carbon dioxide or photosynthetically active radiation? Evaluation of the significance of individual environmental factors that control leaf stomatal development’
content: Stomatal pores in leaves enable CO2 uptake into the plant and control transpiration. Leaf stomatal patterns determine maximal potential for photosynthesis and stomatal water loss, and impact plant productivity and stress tolerance. Thus, it is important that stomatal patterns in leaves develop in accordance with the plant’s growth environment. Stomatal patterns are usually described using stomatal density (the number of stomata per unit leaf area) and stomatal index (proportion of stomata from all epidermal cells). In amphistomatous plants, which produce stomata on both the adaxial (upper) and abaxial (lower) leaf surface, these parameters can be determined for both leaf surfaces and the distribution of stomata between leaf surfaces can be characterized by adaxial-to-abaxial stomatal density ratio (stomatal ratio). Both stomatal density and index depend on the plant growth environment. For example, more stomata are usually produced under higher light levels, and fewer under elevated CO2 concentrations and temperatures (Chua and Lau, 2024; Poorter et al., 2025). Such changes are assumed to optimize gas exchange efficiency and offset environmental stress; however, the driving factors and processes remain unclear. To help address this, Pleva et al. (2025) used sunflower (Helianthus annuus) as a model to understand which factor is more important for stomatal density determination: light or intercellular CO2 concentration (Ci). The authors grew sunflowers under a light gradient and measured Ci of true leaves and stomatal density in the adaxial and abaxial epidermis of both cotyledons and true leaves.
